horoscopes.intro: November 13 in the stars: Find out what’s in store for you today in our daily horoscopes for Friday November 13. Read the daily horoscopes for your Sun sign or rising sign (ascendant) to plan your day.

aries.text: Two planets straighten out today, Aries, which makes this the least cursed Friday the 13th in recent memory. Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio and your eighth house of shared assets, so that stalled negotiation can finally move. Read the fine print before you sign, or hand it to a lawyer and spare yourself the eye strain. Then amorous Venus turns direct this evening in fair-minded Libra and your seventh house of committed relationships, closing six weeks in which every union seemed to hit a valley. Rather than relitigating the whole stretch, try picking the one thing you’d actually like to change and ask for it. And if an ex resurfaced during the backspin, Venus won’t reverse again for 18 months, so you’ve got plenty of time to decide whether they were a lesson or a keeper.

taurus.text: Two planets, including your ruler Venus, end their retrogrades today, Taurus, which is quite a lot of relief for one afternoon. First up, messenger Mercury straightens out in Scorpio and your relationship house, where people have been bafflingly defensive for three weeks. Rather than waiting for the apology you’re owed, try offering the one you’ve been withholding. You’ll be amazed what moves. Ardent Venus also turns direct in Libra and your sixth house of wellbeing, after six weeks that made eating well and working out feel like Sisyphean tasks. Now you’ve got wings to carry you to class. Don’t skip the pampering either, since your sensual sign gets real mileage out of going upscale. Book a good massage and call it maintenance.

gemini.text: Today’s double course correction has both your ruler Mercury and Venus turning direct, lifting a serious weight off your shoulders. As Mercury powers ahead in Scorpio and your sector of work and wellness, the focus you’ve been missing comes back online. Set a real deadline for finishing projects and recommit to regular workouts and healthier eating. Venus also turns direct in your passionate fifth house, wrapping six weeks in which romance either sputtered or refused to start at all. Flirting and fun return in the days ahead. If you’re interested in meeting someone new, try showing up at a few events alone. You’re much more accessible when the interested parties don’t have to elbow past your four closest friends to say hello.

cancer.text: Two retrogrades end at once today, Cancer, and both of them have been working on your heart. Mercury turns direct in Scorpio and your fifth house of passion, so make your intentions clear with whoever has your attention. Rather than hinting and hoping they decode it, try saying it plainly. Later, harmonious Venus straightens out in Libra and your domestic fourth house, where things have been anything BUT peaceful for six weeks. Brew a pot of chai and invite the roommate or relative you clashed with to talk about moving forward instead of relitigating October. A decor refresh wouldn’t hurt either, since fresh paint and new linens can feel like a renovation for a fraction of the price.

leo.text: Both Mercury and Venus turn direct this Friday the 13th, Leo, and the only thing hexed around here was the last three weeks. As Mercury straightens out in Scorpio and your domestic fourth house, it’s safe to call back a contractor, reschedule a delivery and while you’re making calls, ring a relative you’ve been avoiding. (Just skip the part where you rehash who said what.) Social Venus also ends her retrograde in Libra and your chatty third house, after six weeks that strained your friend circle and possibly a sibling relationship. Burying the hatchet gets considerably easier now, and going first costs you nothing. The local scene could heat up with promise so show up and mingle.

virgo.text: Two planets correct course today, Virgo, which should end three weeks of scrambled signals. First up, your ruler Mercury pivots forward in Scorpio and your communication sector, giving you the green light to resend an unanswered email and correct the record where you got misread. If an apology is owed in either direction, go first. Affectionate Venus also ends her retrograde in Libra and your house of emotional and financial stability, closing six weeks that may have brought a monetary rough patch or some insecurity about where you stand with someone. The silver lining? You can stop demanding perfection, starting with the person enforcing the standard (uh, you). Embrace the art of the “beautiful mess.”

libra.text: Two planets turn direct today, Libra, including your ruler Venus, so consider this the luckiest Friday the 13th in recent memory. As Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio and your financial sector, chase an unpaid invoice and get conversations going again about new work. Then tonight, Venus straightens out in your sign, closing six weeks in which your best efforts felt like they were missing the mark. If you took it personally, plenty of Libras did, and you can stop now. With your ruler moving forward through your sign, you’ll feel ready to say what you actually think instead of editing yourself for the room. Follow a creative whim while you’re at it. This could be your magnum opus!

scorpio.text: Sweet, sweet relief! A double course correction arrives today, Scorpio, as both Mercury and Venus end their retrogrades—both of which hit YOUR sign. As messenger Mercury straightens out in Scorpio, so your words get their precision back. Sensual Venus also wraps a six-week reverse that began in your sign on October 3 before slipping into Libra and your twelfth house on October 25. Since then, you’ve likely been keeping your own counsel and possibly your distance. Reach back out to whoever you withdrew from. You don’t owe them a lengthy explanation, but you might want to offer an apology in the name of mending fences.

sagittarius.text: Two retrogrades end today, Sag, great news for Friday the 13th. Mindful Mercury straightens out in your twelfth house after three weeks of unusually heavy introspection. Get ready for clarity to roll in, and it may well be about access. If you’ve been too available to someone who only reaches out when they need something, start putting up boundaries. Vixen Venus also turns direct in your friendship sector, closing six weeks that could have left you feeling oddly disconnected. A good friendship may have hit the skids, or a promising romance got filed under platonic. Either way, skip the post-mortem. Text the friend who went quiet and get a meetup on the calendar, and you’ll have your answer soon enough.

capricorn.text: Both Mercury and Venus turn direct today, Capricorn, which is more good news than Friday the 13th usually delivers. Communal Mercury ends its retrograde in your eleventh house of teamwork, so that collaboration stuck in limbo since October can finally move. Have you been spinning your wheels with people? Instead of trying to force an alliance, this could be your cue to break free and search for greener pastures. Amiable Venus also straightens out in your career corner, where a few key objectives got punted to the sidelines. Starting now, you can roll up your sleeves and blast full speed ahead. Romantically, it’s a fine moment to resume those “next steps” conversations, just don’t come off too heavy. And if you’re playing for keeps, the commitmentphobes don’t deserve your time of day.

aquarius.text: Two planets end their retrogrades today, Aquarius, so those red lights you kept hitting finally turn green. Mercury straightens out in your determined tenth house, which means you can hit the gas without worrying you’ll stall out. Keep cranking out high-quality work, but know that unseen hands may come to your aid, whether that’s a supportive exec who helps you rise through the ranks or a coveted assignment that puts your name on the map. Vixen Venus also turns direct in your expansive ninth house, where your love life may have gone MIA for the past six weeks. Whether you’re single or spoken for, you’ll benefit from a change of scenery. Start circulating in new venues and think about booking a trip to the place where the natural scenery includes human eye candy!

pisces.text: Two planets correct course today, Pisces, and Friday the 13th has rarely looked so lucky! Mercury ends its retrograde in your expansive ninth house, so set your GPS coordinates and hit the accelerator on the long-range plans that got scrambled last month. This house also governs honesty, and if someone’s been playing fast and loose with the truth, the wool starts lifting from your eyes. Don’t go flinging accusations. You need solid proof, an airtight case AND an open mind, because for all you know it was an innocent misunderstanding. Sensual Venus also turns direct in your eighth house of intimacy, closing six weeks in which you either saw a new side of someone or caught a sudden case of cold feet about a dalliance that was just heating up. Don’t go into denial about whatever surfaces now. Facing an inconvenient truth is no picnic, but isn’t it better than living a lie?

items.abstract: It is highly desirable to design and engineer lightweight, low-power-consumption, and rapid physical intelligence (PI) structures that couple with multiple robotic functions. Here, we present a multimodal electromechanical switch (mEMS), consisting of a stretchable droplet-amplified electrostatic zipping structure, a convex bump, and a pair of electrical contacts, that can be used to achieve the widely used mechanical momentary, mechanical latching, and electrically actuated switching modes by simply tuning the applied voltage and using the same structure. We theoretically investigate the snap-through behavior of the elastic zipping membrane, which can be used to endow the mEMS with voltage-dependent memory, and the theoretical considerations are experimentally validated. As a result, we can apply the mEMS array for robotic memory, such as information writing and erasing; robotic communication by reprogrammable information encrypting, decrypting, and display; robotic computation by electrically reprogrammable logic gates; and reprogrammable binary information transferring. The mEMS represents a comprehensive PI structure for next-generation autonomous machines that can better adapt in unstructured and complex real-world environments.

items.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
items.originalTitle: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
items.summary: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1-8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1-8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

items.title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
items.originalTitle: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
items.summary: The cellular and molecular bases of inter-individual variation in the human brain are not yet understood, particularly beyond the neocortex. 9 million nuclei from 178 adult brain donors.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: The cellular and molecular bases of inter-individual variation in the human brain are not yet understood, particularly beyond the neocortex. Here, we describe cellular and gene-expression variation in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) analysis of 3.9 million nuclei from 178 adult brain donors. People with more astrocytes, microglia, or oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in any one brain region tended to have this property in all gray-matter regions sampled. OPC proportions declined by 40% across ages 30-80 in the cortex and striatum. Age-associated gene-expression changes differed substantially across cell types. Donor age was predicted from RNA-expression patterns with a median absolute error of 6.6 years across cell types. Common genetic variants were associated with the expression of nearly 10,000 genes; these effects were mostly cell-type specific and distinguished striatal from cortical neurons. These open-access data provide a foundation for future studies of human brain variation and vulnerabilities.

items.title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia
items.originalTitle: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia
items.summary: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

items.title: Asymmetric cell division is predictive of human T cell vaccine responses
items.originalTitle: Asymmetric cell division is predictive of human T cell vaccine responses
items.summary: Vaccine-induced protection relies on the generation and maintenance of stem-like memory B and T cells, a process sustained by two conserved mechanisms: asymmetric cell division (ACD) and autophagy.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Vaccine-induced protection relies on the generation and maintenance of stem-like memory B and T cells, a process sustained by two conserved mechanisms: asymmetric cell division (ACD) and autophagy. In T cells, ACD enables them to produce progeny with the same T cell receptor but with divergent metabolic and functional fates upon antigen encounter through the unequal inheritance of cellular cargoes. Autophagy recycles cellular components, provides metabolic substrates essential for sustaining energy demands, and is relevant for the maintenance of T cell memory. Direct evidence of how these processes synergize and affect human immunity is still lacking. Here, we show that mitotic human CD8+ T cells asymmetrically segregate autophagy-related organelles, including autophagosomes and lysosomes. Furthermore, we show that ACD drives divergent transcriptional and functional fates in daughter cells. Extending these findings to an influenza vaccine trial, we demonstrate that autophagic flux follows the dynamics of clonal expansion and contraction of antigen-specific T cells. Notably, individuals with enhanced ACD capacity, especially with increased LC3B asymmetry, exhibit better vaccine responses, linking early cellular segregation events to long-term immune fitness. Last, transient use of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 inhibitor rapamycin improved memory survival, which was associated with improved ACD, measured by the asymmetric inheritance of both CD8 and LC3B. Together, these findings highlight that the asymmetric inheritance of the autophagy machinery represents another layer of human adaptive immunity and offers a potential therapeutic target to enhance vaccine outcomes.

items.title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain
items.originalTitle: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain
items.summary: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. Here, we present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas by jointly profiling the transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) or repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 adult brain regions. We targeted over 750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrated these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptomes. This framework resolved chromatin states for over 500,000 candidate regulatory elements, identified enhancer-gene links and regulatory programs, revealed Polycomb-associated ultra-long-range contacts, and uncovered brainwide epigenomic heterogeneity. We further developed a sequence-to-function model to predict cell-type-specific effects of candidate neurological disease variants. Finally, comparative analyses across species reveal conservation in active regulatory programs but divergence in repressive programs. Together, this study provides a comprehensive epigenomic reference for interpreting regulatory principles and epigenetic memory underlying human brain organization and disease.

items.title: Optimizing exercise prescriptions for improving neuropsychiatric symptoms in older adults with MCI or dementia: a dose-response meta-analysis
items.originalTitle: Optimizing exercise prescriptions for improving neuropsychiatric symptoms in older adults with MCI or dementia: a dose-response meta-analysis
items.summary: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia are common among older adults and are often accompanied by neuropsychiatric symptoms, which negatively affect quality of life and functional independence.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia are common among older adults and are often accompanied by neuropsychiatric symptoms, which negatively affect quality of life and functional independence. Although exercise is a promising non-pharmacological intervention, the effective dose ranges for different exercise modalities in improving neuropsychiatric symptoms remain unclear. This study aimed to examine the dose-response relationships between different exercise modalities and neuropsychiatric symptoms among older adults with MCI or dementia.

Methods: Exercise dose was calculated as the product of duration, frequency, and intensity, expressed as metabolic equivalent of task minutes per week (MET-min/week). Bayesian network and dose-response meta-analyses were conducted to compare the effects of different exercise modalities and characterize their dose-response relationships.

Results: Nineteen studies involving 1587 older adults with MCI or dementia were included. Overall exercise showed a U-shaped dose-response association with improvements in neuropsychiatric symptoms, with the greatest effect observed at approximately 490 MET-min/week (SMD = -0.51, 95% CrI: -0.91, -0.08). When stratified by exercise modality, aerobic exercise (8 arms), resistance training (4 arms), and mind-body exercise (7 arms) were significantly associated with improvements in neuropsychiatric symptoms, although their effective and optimal doses varied across modalities. The doses associated with the model-identified greatest effects were 460 MET-min/week for aerobic exercise (SMD = -0.53, 95% CrI: -0.76, -0.24; very low certainty evidence), 470 MET-min/week for resistance training (SMD = -0.49, 95% CrI: -0.76, -0.17; very low certainty evidence), and 490 MET-min/week for mind-body exercise (SMD = -0.63, 95% CrI: -0.94, -0.28; low certainty evidence). No significant moderating effects were identified in network meta-regression analyses.

Conclusion: Aerobic exercise, resistance training, and mind-body exercise showed distinct dose-response relationships for improving neuropsychiatric symptoms in older adults with MCI or dementia. However, given the very low to low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm these findings.

Systematic review registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261486763, identifier CRD420261486763.

items.title: Invasive versus conservative strategy for older patients with myocardial infarction based on cognitive function: the SENIOR-RITA cognition analysis
items.originalTitle: Invasive versus conservative strategy for older patients with myocardial infarction based on cognitive function: the SENIOR-RITA cognition analysis
items.summary: Older adults with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and cognitive impairment experience higher cardiovascular risk than patients with normal cognition. It remains unclear how cognition should influence whether older adults receive an invasive or conservative treatment strategy.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Older adults with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and cognitive impairment experience higher cardiovascular risk than patients with normal cognition. It remains unclear how cognition should influence whether older adults receive an invasive or conservative treatment strategy.

Objectives: To compare an invasive and conservative treatment strategy among older adults with NSTEMI and cognitive impairment.

Methods: This study is a pre-specified analysis of the SENIOR-RITA randomised controlled trial. Cognition was measured at randomisation using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Patients were followed up for a median of 4.1 years postrandomisation. The primary outcome was a composite of time to cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI).

Results: MoCA was available for 1455 patients (95.8%) who underwent randomisation. Within the cognitively impaired group (909 patients), the primary outcome occurred in 116 patients (26.8%) in the invasive group and in 141 patients (29.6%) in the conservative group (hazard ratio [HR], 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.10; P = 0.20). Nonfatal MI occurred in 48 patients (11.1%) in the invasive group and in 75 patients (15.8%) in the conservative group (HR 0.64; 95% CI, 0.44 to 0.92). However, there was no interaction between treatment strategy and cognition.

Conclusions: Among those with evidence of cognitive impairment at randomisation, an invasive treatment strategy did not reduce the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI, and there was no evidence of treatment effect heterogeneity based on cognition. The reduction in nonfatal MI events among those with cognitive impairment should be interpreted as an exploratory finding.

items.title: Brain-wide pathways for object identity and location are dominated by internal strategies
items.originalTitle: Brain-wide pathways for object identity and location are dominated by internal strategies
items.summary: , 'what' and 'where' streams). Here, using the mouse whisker system, we demonstrate an existence of two alternating brain-wide (beyond cortex) subnetworks that are primarily driven by internal strategies, rather than external parameters.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: It is long thought that higher-order sensory processing is divided into two specialized cortical streams that encode in parallel either the identity of an object or its location (i.e., 'what' and 'where' streams). Here, using the mouse whisker system, we demonstrate an existence of two alternating brain-wide (beyond cortex) subnetworks that are primarily driven by internal strategies, rather than external parameters. We combine simultaneous brain-wide neuronal recordings in male mice trained to identify or locate a certain stimulus. We find that mice deploy either an active search or a passive sensation strategy during task performance. These strategies respectively drive two distinct brain-wide subnetworks, frontal and posterior related to an active and passive strategy respectively. Using a computational framework, we show that the posterior subnetwork encoded additional internal strategic parameters such as trial history, the first task of the day, and training history. When discarding the dominance of the frontal subnetwork, specific areas within the posterior subnetwork encoded meaningful task information regarding object identity and location. Integrated together, these two subnetworks may comprise optimal sensory integration.
